cards.title: Find the airport bottleneck
cards.hook: More passengers do not help if one part of the airport cannot handle them.
cards.lead: UCL describes ICARUS as running a troubled airport, balancing passenger flow, terminal capacity, commercial income and expansion.
sections: Capacity is connected
A decision to attract more airlines changes passenger demand. Check whether gates, terminal space and staff can absorb it before assuming revenue will rise.
Make one forecast
Before a round, write down the constraint you expect to bind first, the metric that would reveal it, and the action you would take if it appears.
cards.takeaway: A stronger decision explains how capacity and demand move together.
cards.q: Demand rises but terminal capacity is already tight. What should your team test first?
cards.prompt: Name one airport metric you would watch before expanding demand.

cards.title: Run a decision log each round
cards.hook: A good team can say what it expected, what happened and what it will change.
cards.lead: The UCL ICARUS competition used successive decision rounds and reports. Treat each round as a small strategy experiment.
sections: Before you submit
Agree on the objective, one or two critical assumptions and who checks the numbers. Record the expected effect of each major decision.
After results arrive
Compare forecasts with actual passenger satisfaction, utilisation, cash and commercial income. Diagnose a miss before changing several levers at once.
cards.takeaway: Write a prediction before a decision, then learn from the variance.
cards.q: Which team habit makes the next ICARUS round more informative?
cards.prompt: Write one prediction and one metric for an ICARUS decision.

cards.title: Make the trade-off explicit
cards.hook: A premium strategy and a low-cost strategy imply different choices.
cards.lead: UCL lists commercial income, passenger flow, terminal capacity and expansion among the levers in ICARUS. A coherent team strategy links them.
sections: Choose a direction
State whom the airport serves and how it earns money. Consider whether services, capacity and investment match that positioning.
Watch second-order effects
Extra retail income may depend on passenger time and satisfaction. Expansion can raise capacity but absorb cash before its benefits appear.
cards.takeaway: One coherent strategy beats a collection of attractive but conflicting moves.
cards.q: Your team targets fast low-cost transfers. Which decision needs most scrutiny?
options: A capacity plan supporting short connections
A measurement plan for waiting times
cards.prompt: Explain a trade-off between revenue and passenger experience.

cards.title: Build–Measure–Learn in one commute
cards.hook: Turn a risky assumption into a test you can run this week.
cards.lead: The MSc pre-start reading list recommends The Lean Startup by Eric Ries (or All in Startup by Diana Kander). Ries frames startup progress as Build–Measure–Learn: test an assumption, observe customer behaviour, then decide what to change.
sections: Start with the assumption
For ForBrewers, a hypothesis might be that a brewery places a second direct order without repeated founder persuasion.
Specify the evidence
Pick a measurable behaviour, a time window and a threshold before launching the experiment. An interview compliment is weaker than an actual paid repeat order.
cards.takeaway: The loop is useful only when the measurement can change your decision.
cards.q: Which result best tests repeat demand for ForBrewers?
options: Paid repeat orders from independent breweries
cards.prompt: Write one falsifiable assumption and the customer behaviour that would test it.

cards.title: An MVP is a learning tool
cards.hook: The smallest useful test is the one that answers the important question.
cards.lead: Ries describes the MVP as a way to gain validated customer learning with the least effort; it need not be a polished miniature of the final product.
sections: Design backwards
Ask what you need to learn. If the unknown is whether breweries buy directly, a manual offer and actual transaction can test it before a full marketplace exists.
Do not optimise for tiny
A too-thin prototype that cannot reveal genuine customer behaviour wastes time. Keep exactly enough to get reliable feedback.
cards.takeaway: Minimum refers to effort needed for learning, not arbitrary feature count.
options: It looks like a finished app
It yields evidence about a risky assumption
cards.prompt: Describe a low-effort test for one uncertain part of your venture.
cards.sourceLabel: Eric Ries · What is an MVP?

cards.title: Interview about behaviour, not praise
cards.hook: A story about a past purchase is more useful than a guess about a future one.
cards.lead: UCL puts customer discovery and lean experimentation at the start of the MSc. Use induction week to practise asking neutral, specific questions.
sections: Ask for an episode
What happened the last time you bought hops? Who approved it, what took time, and what alternative did you consider?
Separate observation from inference
Record what the person actually did and said. Save your interpretation for later so a team can challenge it.
cards.takeaway: Concrete past behaviour is a better starting point than a polite prediction.
options: How did you handle your last purchase?
Will you definitely buy next month?
cards.prompt: Write one neutral question you could ask a founder or brewery buyer.

cards.title: Profit is not cash
cards.hook: A sale can look good in a P&L while the bank balance is still falling.
cards.lead: The programme reading list calls Entrepreneurial Finance, 2nd ed., by Simon Hulme with Chris Drew and Mauricio Pettinato Lucio essential for the finance module. Its three-statement introduction helps separate reported profit from actual cash timing.
sections: Timing matters
A customer may pay later while the supplier must be paid now. The sale increases reported revenue but cash does not arrive yet.
Use a simple bridge
For a ForBrewers order, note when the brewery pays, when the hop processing and freight bills fall due, and how much working capital is tied up.
cards.takeaway: Track when money moves, not only whether a deal is profitable.
cards.q: A profitable order is paid by the buyer in 60 days; the supplier is due today. What is the immediate risk?
cards.prompt: Explain in one sentence why a profitable order might still strain cash.

cards.title: Three statements, three questions
cards.hook: P&L, balance sheet and cash flow tell related but different stories.
cards.lead: The publisher describes Hulme’s text as guiding finance newcomers through all three statements.
sections: P&L
Was the activity profitable over a period after matching revenue and expenses?
Balance sheet
What does the business own and owe at a specific point? Cash flow asks what cash entered and left during the period.
cards.takeaway: Use the right statement for the question you are answering.
cards.q: Where would you first check whether cash actually arrived this month?
cards.prompt: Give one example of a question answered by the balance sheet.

cards.title: Fund the next proof
cards.hook: Tie spending to the uncertainty the venture must resolve next.
cards.lead: UCL’s MSc includes Entrepreneurial Finance and hands-on venture development. Make each funding request explain what it will prove.
sections: Milestone first
An early venture could use a small budget to demonstrate repeat demand before paying to automate fulfilment.
Measure runway honestly
Write down current cash, monthly net burn, the cost of the test and the decision date. Then identify what evidence would justify further investment.
cards.takeaway: Finance a defined learning milestone rather than an abstract ambition.
cards.q: What is the strongest use of a first small budget?
options: An experiment with a decision threshold
A full launch with no metrics
cards.prompt: State the next piece of evidence you would want before scaling ForBrewers.

cards.title: Make the first team meeting useful
cards.hook: A small decision process helps strangers become a working team quickly.
cards.lead: UCL describes the MSc as highly collaborative, with customer discovery, prototypes and pitches. Use the first exercise to establish how your group decides.
sections: Agree on roles for one round
Assign a timekeeper, a numbers checker and a person who records assumptions. Rotate roles next time rather than fixing them forever.
Invite the quietest signal
Ask each person for one risk before deciding. A different background may reveal a constraint the loudest person missed.
cards.takeaway: Leave the meeting with one decision, one owner and one thing to measure.
cards.q: Which next step makes the team’s decision more testable?
options: Record the assumption, owner and metric
Let the loudest member decide alone
cards.prompt: Write one sentence you could say to help your new team decide well.

cards.title: Make a mixed team legible
cards.hook: Your first group decision can fail even when everyone agrees on the goal.
cards.lead: The MSc reading list recommends Erin Meyer’s The Culture Map to understand an international cohort. Her framework compares communication and decision habits across cultures; an individual may differ from a national pattern.
sections: Make the process explicit
Before an ICARUS round, agree who voices options, when objections are invited and who records the final decision. Ask rather than assume how teammates prefer to disagree.
Confirm the decision
End with a written choice, one reason, and the metric you will check. This reduces ambiguity when communication styles differ.
cards.takeaway: Treat cultural patterns as prompts for conversation, never as labels for a person.
cards.q: What best checks that an international team has agreed on a simulation move?
options: Write the decision and ask each teammate to flag a concern
Let one person speak for everyone
cards.prompt: Write a sentence that invites a dissenting view before your team submits a choice.

cards.topic: Building High Impact Ventures · Value Proposition Design
cards.title: Match a job to a benefit
cards.hook: Features matter when they solve a specific customer job or pain.
cards.lead: The MSc reading list recommends Value Proposition Design by Alexander Osterwalder and coauthors. Its canvas pairs a customer profile—jobs, pains, gains—with the product’s pain relievers and gain creators.
sections: Begin with one customer segment
For a brewery buyer, the job may be to source reliable ingredients on time; a pain may be uncertain delivery or fragmented quotes. Write what you have actually heard.
Test the claimed fit
Match one offer to one important pain, then ask buyers for evidence. A neat canvas alone cannot validate a market.
cards.takeaway: Prioritise the strongest job–benefit match and test it with the customer.
cards.q: What is strongest evidence of value proposition fit?
options: A buyer repeatedly uses or pays for the offer that solves a priority pain
cards.prompt: Name one customer job and one specific way your offer helps.

cards.title: Test a growth channel cheaply
cards.hook: Reach to buyers is an experiment, not a list of marketing ideas.
cards.lead: The MSc reading list recommends Traction by Gabriel Weinberg and Justin Mares for Entrepreneurial Marketing, Strategy and Branding. Its channel framework encourages testing ways to reach customers before concentrating spend.
sections: Choose plausible channels
ForBrewers might compare direct outreach to breweries with a relevant trade-event introduction. Define the audience and effort for each small test.
Compare a meaningful result
Measure qualified conversations or paid orders per unit of time and money—not impressions alone. Double down only when one channel shows useful traction.
cards.takeaway: Run small comparable tests, then focus on the channel that produces the right customers.
cards.q: Which metric best helps compare two early B2B channels?
options: Qualified buyer conversations per £ and hour
cards.prompt: Suggest two channels and one metric to compare them fairly.

cards.title: Fundamental British Values
cards.hook: Democracy, law, liberty and respect are principles you can use in a diverse university community.
cards.lead: The Department for Education names democracy, the rule of law, individual liberty, and mutual respect and tolerance of people with different faiths and beliefs. These principles support participation and freedom alongside equal treatment.
sections: In a seminar
Let others challenge an idea, use agreed decision rules, and distinguish disagreement from denying someone equal participation. Respect does not require agreement.
cards.takeaway: Democracy, law, liberty and respect are principles you can use in a diverse university community.
cards.q: Which response best reflects these principles in a team?
options: Require everyone to share one belief
Let everyone participate, debate and follow fair rules
cards.prompt: Explain how you would combine freedom of expression with mutual respect in a UCL discussion.
cards.provenance: Supplementary primary-source concepts for MSc entrepreneurship; not a claim of assigned UCL reading.

cards.title: Make the hypothesis falsifiable
cards.hook: A test is useful only if its result could change your mind.
cards.lead: A strong business hypothesis states one specific belief, a relevant customer group and an observable outcome. Separate willingness to pay from ease of use so one result cannot conceal failure in the other.
sections: Before the test
Write what outcome would disconfirm the belief, then choose an experiment capable of observing it. A precise test makes evidence easier to interpret.
cards.takeaway: A test is useful only if its result could change your mind.
cards.q: Which hypothesis is easiest to test?
options: At least 4 of 10 target buyers will place a paid trial order
cards.prompt: Write one testable hypothesis for a venture and the outcome that would make you reconsider it.
cards.provenance: Supplementary primary-source concepts for MSc entrepreneurship; not a claim of assigned UCL reading.

cards.title: Test the riskiest assumption first
cards.hook: Polishing a prototype is low value if the basic demand assumption is false.
cards.lead: Rank assumptions by how uncertain they are and how damaging failure would be. Test the critical uncertain belief before committing resources to less consequential details.
sections: Choose the experiment
If demand is uncertain, observe a concrete customer commitment before improving surface design. The cheapest useful test addresses the belief that could overturn the whole idea.
cards.takeaway: Polishing a prototype is low value if the basic demand assumption is false.
options: A small test of a critical uncertain demand assumption
A full product build before any customer contact
A test of something already known
cards.prompt: Name your most dangerous uncertain assumption and a cheap experiment that could invalidate it.
cards.provenance: Supplementary primary-source concepts for MSc entrepreneurship; not a claim of assigned UCL reading.

cards.title: Start from the means you have
cards.hook: Who you are, what you know and who you know can shape the next feasible step.
cards.lead: The bird-in-hand principle of effectuation starts with existing means instead of requiring a fully predicted market. Your knowledge, identity and relationships help you choose actions you can take now.
sections: A practical move
List your means, then identify a small action that becomes possible with them. A partner commitment can extend what you can do next.
cards.takeaway: Who you are, what you know and who you know can shape the next feasible step.
options: Starting with existing knowledge, identity and relationships
Waiting until every resource is available
cards.prompt: Describe one venture action you can take using what you already know or the people you already know.
cards.provenance: Supplementary primary-source concepts for MSc entrepreneurship; not a claim of assigned UCL reading.

cards.title: Set an affordable-loss boundary
cards.hook: Decide what you can lose before an uncertain experiment begins.
cards.lead: The affordable-loss principle bounds the resources committed to an action rather than relying only on predicted upside. Include time and effort as well as money.
sections: Make the limit explicit
Choose the experiment and a loss you can absorb. When the boundary is reached, use the evidence to decide whether another bounded step is justified.
cards.takeaway: Decide what you can lose before an uncertain experiment begins.
options: Commit everything because returns look large
Keep investing to recover sunk costs
Set a tolerable resource limit before an uncertain test
cards.prompt: Give a maximum amount of time or money you can afford to lose on one venture experiment and explain why.
cards.provenance: Supplementary primary-source concepts for MSc entrepreneurship; not a claim of assigned UCL reading.

cards.title: Match the evidence to the claim
cards.hook: A compliment and a real customer action answer different questions.
cards.lead: Choose an experiment that can observe the specific belief you are testing. Direct observation offers context, while a less mediated test can reduce the effect of your presence on customer behaviour.
sections: Interpret carefully
A positive response is useful evidence of that response. It does not automatically establish repeated use or paid demand. State the narrower conclusion the experiment supports.
cards.takeaway: A compliment and a real customer action answer different questions.
cards.q: Which conclusion is warranted after people praise a concept?
options: They gave a positive response; further behavioural evidence is needed
cards.prompt: Explain what one customer experiment can establish and what it still leaves uncertain.
cards.provenance: Supplementary primary-source concepts for MSc entrepreneurship; not a claim of assigned UCL reading.
